parole.testo: From Old Spanish averar, from Early Medieval Latin advērāre. The /d/ was (re-)inserted due to Latin influence.
Inherited from Early Medieval Latin allūmināre. Compare Portuguese alumiar.

Inherited from Early Medieval Latin andāre. The preterite's origin is unclear, most likely generalized from the preterite of haber (“to have”), hub- (note that b and v are pronounced identically; compare the same development in tener, and more alike to this verb, estar).
Inherited from Early Medieval Latin adrīpāre. Synchronically a- + riba + -ar.

Inherited from Early Medieval Latin blancus, from Proto-Germanic *blankaz (“white, bright, blinding”), from Proto-Indo-European *bhleg- (“to shine”). Found as early as the Cantar de Mio Cid. Compare Old High German blanch (“shining, bright, white”) (German blank), Old English blanc (“white, grey”),
Inherited from Old Spanish calça, from Early Medieval Latin calcea, from Latin calceus + -a.

parole.significato: hood, especially a kind worn as a popular outfit in certain regions
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish capiello, from Early Medieval Latin cappellus, diminutive from Late Latin cappa. Doublet of chapeo and chapó (from French) as well as capelo (from Italian). Compare English chapeau.
From ceño (“frown, scowl; brow”) + -ar, or from Early Medieval Latin cinnāre (“to blink”).
From Early Medieval Latin dēsideus (“desire”), from Latin dēsidia (“sloth, debauchery”).
Inherited from Old Spanish desfazer, from Early Medieval Latin disfacere. Synchronically des- + hacer.

parole.significato: to throw, toss, cast, jettison (to release an object from one's grasp so that it moves through the air)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish echar, from Early Medieval Latin iectāre, from Classical Latin iactāre. Doublet of the borrowing jactar. Cognate with Catalan gitar, Galician xeitar, French jeter, Portuguese jeito, and Sicilian jittari; alongside more distantly English jet and jut.

parole.significato: to worsen, to make worse, to exacerbate
parole.testo: From Early Medieval Latin impeiōrāre, from Latin peiōrem (“worse”). By surface analysis, en- + peor + -ar.
Inherited from Early Medieval Latin examplāre (with Spanish prefix en-), from Latin amplus.

parole.significato: woodland, greenwood, dell, forest (dense collection of trees)
parole.testo: Ultimately from Early Medieval Latin foresta. Influenced by flor (“flower”).
Ultimately from Early Medieval Latin foresta.
From Early Medieval Latin fraxinēta, plural of fraxinētum, derived from Latin fraxinus (“ash tree”).
Inherited from Old Spanish ganar, from Early Medieval Latin ganāre, q.v.

parole.significato: to save (to store for future use)
parole.testo: Inherited from Early Medieval Latin wardāre.
Inherited from Early Medieval Latin warnīre.
Inherited from Old Spanish guerra, from Early Medieval Latin werra, borrowed from Frankish *werʀu (“confusion; quarrel”).
From Early Medieval Latin gelāta, derived from Latin gelāre (“freeze”). By surface analysis, helar + -ada.
Inherited from Old Spanish herbadgo, hervadgo, ervadgo (c. 1257), Early Medieval Latin herbāticum, from Latin herba (“grass”). By surface analysis, hierba + -azgo. Doublet of herbaje.

parole.significato: handle (part of an object which is held in the hand)
parole.testo: From Early Medieval Latin manicus, derived from Latin manus (“hand”).
Inherited from Early Medieval Latin medālia. Doublet of medalla.
Inherited from Old Spanish montanna, from Early Medieval Latin montānia, a collective based on Latin montem.
From Early Medieval Latin auctōricāre. Cf. Portuguese outorgar.
Inherited from Early Medieval Latin patrīnus (“godfather”), from Latin pater (“father”).
Inherited from Old Spanish parlar (1293), borrowed from Gallo-Romance (cf. Catalan and Occitan parlar, French parler), from Early Medieval Latin parabolāre.
Inherited from Early Medieval Latin pollicipēs, from pollex (“thumb”) + pēs (“foot”).
Derived from Early Medieval Latin rendita. Compare Galician renda, Portuguese renda.
Inherited from Early Medieval Latin rīpāria.

parole.significato: rein(s) (strap or rope attached to a bridle or bit and used to control an animal, especially a horse)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish rienda (“reins”, often singular), inherited from Early Medieval Latin retina (via */ˈrɛd(e)na/, with metathesis of /dn/; compare Spanish candado < cadnado < Latin catēnātum), a noun derived from Latin retinēre (“hold back, restrain”). Compare Portuguese rédea.

parole.significato: trail, path, track (a route for travel over land)
parole.testo: From Early Medieval Latin sēmitārius, derived from Latin sēmita. Compare Portuguese sendeiro.

From Early Medieval Latin essere, from Latin esse. The form sois pl (“you are”) derives from a Vulgar Latin *sutis. Along the way, the verb absorbed Old Spanish seer < Latin sedēre (“sit”). The present subjunctive may either be from the latter verb (Latin sedeām > Old Spanish *seya > modern Spanish
From Old Spanish solamientre, from Early Medieval Latin sōlā mente. Synchronically derivable from sola + -mente.
Inherited from Early Medieval Latin or Late Latin terrārius, from Latin terra.

Inherited from Early Medieval Latin or Late Latin tenda, from Vulgar Latin *tendita, substantivized feminine of *tenditus, as a variant form of tentus, perfect passive participle of Latin tendō. Compare Italian tenda, Portuguese tenda, Catalan tenda, French tente, Romanian tindă, English tent.
Inherited from Early Medieval Latin ūsāre.
Inherited from Early Medieval Latin vaccārius.

parole.significato: poison (substance that is harmful or lethal to a living organism)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish venino, from Early Medieval Latin venīnum, from Classical Latin venēnum. The modern Spanish form was modified to match the original Latin.
Inherited from Early Medieval Latin verēda (“path, main road”), from Latin verēdus (“light breed of horse”), borrowed from Gaulish *werēdos, from Proto-Celtic *uɸoreidos, from *uɸo- + *reidos.
Inherited from Old Spanish vestidura, from Early Medieval Latin vestītūra.
Borrowed from Italian legname or Old Catalan lenyam (modern llenyam); either way from Early Medieval Latin lignāmen.

Inherited from Old Spanish mesclar, from Early Medieval Latin misculāre, derived from Latin miscēre. Its evolution, like that of Portuguese miscrar, is somewhat unexpected. Compare macho < Latin masculus, with early -scul- > -scl- > /t͡ʃ/. It may be that syncope occurred relatively late for misculār

By dissimilation from an older *temoroso, from temor, or possibly an Early Medieval Latin or Late Latin timorōsus, from Latin timor. Compare Portuguese temeroso, Catalan and Occitan temorós, Italian timoroso and English timorous.
